title: A very short space of time through very short times of space
html_source:
Joyce isolates this abstract thought from action and the world, by omitting verbs and sandwiching it between both sides of the senses.

The simplicity of the words are transformed into a whole without apparent meaning . It hooks us into Stephen’s mind – we become Stephen as the intrigue stays with us moving onto the next lines.

Joyce has already established Stephen as a hero. (Note that the initial incarnation of Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was called Stephen Hero – part of whose manuscript Nora Joyce rescued from a fire after James Joyce had thrown it in. This story is considered apocryphal, however.) He calmly dealt with Mulligan’s attempt to destabilise him in ‘Telemachus’. He stood up to Deasy’s anti-Semitic outburst in ‘Nestor’, and attempted to help a pupil who made an idiot of himself in the same chapter. This sentence, along with colloquialisms elsewhere (‘Open your eyes. No. Jesus!.’), endear Stephen to us. We need this attachment to him now, with there being some disquieting thoughts coming up – not to mention the challenge of negotiating Scylla and Charibdis.
